## Measurement

What's common across every routine at every level, regardless of that
table:

- **Data stays on GPU** — vectors/matrices are allocated with

(C) before the
  timed loop. The measured time is pure compute; no host↔device transfer
  is included.
- **GPU time, not wall time** —

enables WebGPU
  timestamp queries, and each call returns its

, so the JS
  benchmark measures GPU execution, not the CPU-side await overhead. The
  cuBLAS side times each call with a

), so their result
  stays on the GPU — in the default host mode the scalar's copy back to the
  host and the implicit sync would land inside the event window, while the
  wgblas timestamps exclude readback.
- **Full clocks before every configuration** — each size (and each sweep
  value) calls

(C) just
  before its warmup loop. The timed loops wait on every call, so with short
  kernels the GPU is mostly idle and the driver drops to a low-power state
  mid-sweep — on a GTX 1650, memory-bound configurations ran up to ~16×
  slower downclocked (sgemv 1024×2048 transposed: 0.975 ms vs 0.060 ms).
  Locking clocks would fix it but needs root; instead a memory-bound burst
  runs until two timed batches in a row are within 10% of the fastest seen,
  i.e. the memory clock is back at its peak. See

for details.
- **Timed iterations are individually timed; the median is recorded.**
  Median suppresses outliers from OS scheduler preemption better than mean.
  An iteration whose timestamp comes back non-finite or zero is dropped.
- **Configurations that don't fit are skipped, not failed** — where a
  buffer could outgrow the device (large strides, padded leading
  dimensions, f64), the JS side checks

plus, for the f64 routines that stage two
  host copies, available host RAM. A skip is printed and leaves a gap in
  the results rather than a crash.

  just memory-bound, so they additionally report GFLOP/s: sgemm's is

- **Efficiency** — the results tables compare against cuBLAS as

  this is just the ratio of median times: 100% is parity, above 100% means
  wgblas was faster.

## What is BLAS?

BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) is a standard API for vector and
matrix operations — dot products, norms, scalar multiplies, matrix-vector
products. It is the computational backbone of numerical computing, machine
learning frameworks, and scientific software. The reference spec lives at
[netlib.org/blas](https://www.netlib.org/blas/).

GPUs are well-suited for BLAS: operations like saxpy (y = αx + y) are
embarrassingly parallel — each element is independent — so thousands of GPU
threads can work simultaneously. NVIDIA's
[cuBLAS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/) is the canonical example;
this library applies the same idea to the browser via WebGPU.

## What is WebGPU?

WebGPU is the modern GPU API for JavaScript — shipping in Chrome and Edge
(113+), Safari (26+) and Firefox (141+, Windows first), and available in
Node.js through Dawn (the

npm package, which is what this
library's tests and benchmarks run on). It lets JavaScript programs upload
data to the GPU, run compute programs on it, and read results back —
without plugins or native code.

> **Note:** WGSL has no native

## What is a compute shader?

Each routine runs a **compute shader** written in WGSL (a GPU program that
runs thousands of instances in parallel, each handling a slice of the
work — one element, a strided run of elements, or a tile). WebGPU
has vertex and fragment shaders for graphics too — compute shaders are
specifically for general computation. This library only uses compute shaders,
so we call them simply "shaders" throughout.

A ULP is the gap between two adjacent representable float values at a given
